+def _apply_table(s, table):
+    """
+    Apply a _replace_table to s (one code point per token). A merge can only
+    change s if both of its tokens are present: a token is present only if it
+    was in s initially or a replace minting it changed s, so merges using a
+    token known to be absent are skipped without scanning s.
+    """
+    alive = [False] * (table[-1][4] + 1 if table else 1)
+    n = len(alive)
+    for ch in set(s):
+        o = ord(ch)
+        if o < n:
+            alive[o] = True
+    for ps, c, p0, p1, idx in table:
+        if alive[p0] and alive[p1]:
+            m = len(s)
+            s = s.replace(ps, c)
+            if len(s) != m:
+                alive[idx] = True
+    return s

journal.text:
I read the benchmark harness and the whole minbpe package: basic.py, regex.py, base.py and __init__.py. I also searched the imports, which matched 51 lines. Then I edited basic.py, mainly replacing 5 lines at 211-215 with 25, plus two one-line changes at 240 and 257. In regex.py I changed lines 18, 29-30 and 311-314.

Nothing was measured. I ran no sandbox evaluations, and the session stopped without submitting a candidate. So I have no evidence that any of these edits is correct or faster.

I now believe the hot paths live in basic.py and regex.py, with shared helpers in base.py. I can't claim anything about the effect of what I changed.

Next time I should start by reapplying or re-reading those edits, then run lineage_bench.py in the sandbox before touching anything else. Before going further I need to confirm that encode/decode round-trips still match. If they do, I'll submit one small, measured change rather than several unmeasured ones.
